1% rule.def: Never risking more than 1% of your account on a single trade.

2 and 20.def: A traditional hedge fund and private equity fee: 2% of assets a year plus 20% of profits.

accumulation units.def: A version of a fund that reinvests dividends automatically. Income units pay them out instead.

active investing.def: Picking investments to try to beat a benchmark, usually for higher fees than index funds.

advisory.def: Investment banking work advising companies on deals such as M&A, paid mostly by success fees.

aer.def: Annual Equivalent Rate: a savings rate including compounding over a year, so you can compare accounts fairly.

apprentice wage.def: Pay for an apprentice: at least the apprentice minimum (£8.00 an hour from April 2026) under 19 or in the first year, then the rate for your age.

apr.def: Annual Percentage Rate: the yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and compulsory fees. Lower is cheaper.

ask.def: The lowest price a seller will accept right now: what you pay if you buy. Also called the offer.

asset.def: Something you own that's worth money: savings, shares, a car, a house.

asset allocation.def: How you split your money between shares, bonds and cash. It drives most of a portfolio's risk and return.

asset class.def: A group of investments that behave in similar ways, such as shares, bonds, currencies, commodities or crypto.

asset manager.def: A firm that invests other people's money, such as pensions and funds, for a fee. The buy side.

aum.def: Assets under management: the total value of money a manager invests for clients. Fees are usually a % of it.

auto-enrolment.def: The law that makes employers put eligible staff (22+, earning over £10,000) into a workplace pension automatically.

backtest.def: Applying exact strategy rules to past prices to see how they would have performed.

balance sheet.def: A snapshot of what a company owns (assets), owes (liabilities) and what's left for shareholders (equity) on one date.

bank of england.def: The UK's central bank. It sets Bank Rate and aims to keep inflation at 2%.

bank rate.def: The Bank of England's main interest rate, set by the MPC. Savings, mortgage and loan rates tend to follow it.

bank run.def: Many depositors rushing to withdraw at once, which can break even a healthy bank.

behaviour gap.def: The difference between what funds return and what their investors earn, lost to badly timed buying and selling.

bid.def: The highest price a buyer will pay right now: what you get if you sell.

bills.def: Regular household costs such as energy, water, broadband, phone and insurance. Budget for each as a monthly amount.

bnpl.def: Splitting a purchase into a few payments, often interest-free. It's still debt, and missed payments can hurt your credit file.

bond.def: A loan to a government or company that pays a fixed coupon and returns the face value at maturity.

boutique.def: An independent advisory firm focused on M&A advice, without big lending or trading businesses.

breakout.def: Price pushing clearly through support or resistance. Many breakouts fail and fall back.

broker.def: A middleman that buys and sells on behalf of clients, earning fees, commission or a spread.

budget.def: A plan for your money: what comes in, what goes out on needs and wants, and what's left to save.

buy side.def: Firms that invest money, such as asset managers, pension funds, hedge funds and private equity.

candlestick.def: A chart symbol showing one period's open, high, low and close: a body from open to close, wicks to the high and low.

capital.def: A bank's own money (from shareholders and kept profits) that absorbs losses before depositors are hit.

capital gain.def: The profit when you sell an investment for more than you paid.

cash flow statement.def: Shows the real cash coming in and going out, split into operating, investing and financing.

cash isa.def: A savings account inside an ISA wrapper, so the interest is tax-free.

cfd.def: Contract for difference: a leveraged product where you settle the price change with a provider, without owning the asset.

compound interest.def: Interest that's added to your balance, so next time you earn interest on the interest too.

correlation.def: How closely two investments move together, from −1 (opposite) to 1 (in lockstep).

council tax.def: A yearly charge per home paid to the local council. 25% off if you live alone; full-time students are usually exempt.

coupon.def: The fixed interest a bond pays each year, usually as an amount per £100 of face value.

cpi.def: The Consumer Prices Index: the main UK measure of inflation, worked out by the ONS from the prices of a basket of everyday items.

credit file.def: Your record of borrowing and repayments, kept by Experian, Equifax and TransUnion. Lenders check it when you apply.

credit rating.def: An agency's opinion of how likely a borrower is to repay, from AAA (strongest) down to D (in default).

credit score.def: A number an agency or app works out from your credit file. Lenders use your file and their own rules, not this number.

current account.def: Your everyday bank account for pay coming in and bills and card payments going out. Usually pays little or no interest.

dcf.def: Discounted cash flow: valuing a company by adding up the present value of all its future free cash flow.

dcm.def: Debt capital markets: helping companies and governments raise money by issuing bonds or arranging loans.

deflation.def: Prices in general falling over time.

deposit.def: Money held in a bank account: really a promise from the bank to pay you, recorded in its books.

discipline.def: Following your trading plan when your feelings say not to.

discount rate.def: The yearly return you require for waiting and taking risk, used to turn future cash into today's value.

diversification.def: Spreading money across many investments so one bad result hurts less. Cuts risk without cutting expected return.

dividend.def: Part of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders. Not guaranteed.

drawdown.def: A fall from a previous high to a low, such as the FTSE 100 losing about half in 2007–2009.

duration.def: How sensitive a bond's price is to changes in yields. Longer bonds have higher duration.

earnings per share.def: Net profit divided by the number of shares.

easy-access account.def: A savings account you can pay into and take money from at any time. The rate is usually variable.

ecm.def: Equity capital markets: helping companies raise money by issuing shares, such as IPOs.

edge.def: A genuine, repeatable reason your expected value is positive after all costs.

emergency fund.def: Easy-access savings kept for the unexpected. Guidance suggests three to six months of essential costs.

employer contribution.def: Money your employer pays into your pension on top of your pay. At least 3% of qualifying earnings under auto-enrolment.

enterprise value.def: The price of a whole company: market cap + debt − cash.

etf.def: Exchange-traded fund: a fund that trades on a stock exchange like a share, with prices all day.

ev/ebitda.def: Enterprise value ÷ earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Values a whole company including its debt.

expectancy.def: The average result per trade: win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss, usually in R.

expected value.def: The average result per go over many repeats: chance of winning × win − chance of losing × loss.

fixed-rate saver.def: A savings account (often called a bond) that locks your money away for a set time at a fixed rate.

fractional reserve.def: The textbook idea that banks lend out a multiple of their reserves. The Bank of England calls it misleading today.

free cash flow.def: Cash from the everyday business minus spending on equipment and premises: the cash a company really generates.

fscs.def: The Financial Services Compensation Scheme: pays back savers up to £120,000 per person per banking licence if a UK bank fails.

ftse 100.def: An index of the 100 largest companies on the London Stock Exchange's main market, by market cap.

fund.def: A pot of many investors' money that buys lots of investments at once, run for a yearly fee.

gilt.def: A bond issued by the UK government.

gross pay.def: What you earn before anything is taken off: your salary or hourly rate times hours.

hedge fund.def: A lightly restricted fund for professional investors that can short, borrow and use derivatives.

herding.def: Copying what the crowd is doing, which helps inflate bubbles and deepen panics.

income statement.def: The account showing revenue, costs and profit over a period. Also called the profit and loss account.

index.def: A number that tracks the value of a group of shares, such as the FTSE 100, to show how a market is doing.

index fund.def: A fund that copies an index, holding everything in it in proportion to size. Also called a tracker or passive fund.

inflation.def: The rate at which prices in general rise over time, so the same £1 buys less.

inflation target.def: The 2% CPI inflation rate the government asks the Bank of England to aim for.

interest.def: The price of using money. Savers earn it and borrowers pay it.

interest rate.def: Interest as a percentage of the principal. Nearly always quoted per year.

inversion.def: When short-term yields are higher than long-term yields. Has preceded many US recessions.

investment bank.def: A bank serving companies, governments and big investors: deal advice, raising money and trading.

ipo.def: Initial Public Offering: when a private company first sells shares to the public and lists on a stock exchange.

isa.def: Individual Savings Account: a tax-free wrapper for cash or investments. Nothing inside is taxed.

isa allowance.def: The most you can pay into ISAs in a tax year: £20,000 in 2026/27, across all types. Use it or lose it.

journal review.def: Regularly going back through recorded trades to check results, rule-following and behaviour, then making one change.

junior isa.def: A tax-free account for under-18s, opened by a parent or guardian. The child gets it at 18.

lagging indicator.def: An indicator calculated from past prices, so it reacts after moves have happened.

lbo.def: Leveraged buyout: buying a company largely with borrowed money, repaid from the company's own cash.

lending.def: Banks making loans. In the modern economy each new loan creates a new deposit, which is new money.

leverage.def: Controlling a bigger position than your deposit, which multiplies gains and losses.

lifetime isa.def: An ISA for a first home or later life: open at 18–39, pay in up to £4,000 a year, get a 25% bonus. A 25% charge applies to other withdrawals.

limit order.def: An order that only fills at your chosen price or better.

liquidity.def: How easily something can be bought or sold without moving its price.

loss aversion.def: Feeling losses about twice as strongly as equal gains, which leads to panic selling and holding losers too long.

m&a.def: Mergers and acquisitions: companies buying, selling or joining with other companies.

macd.def: Moving Average Convergence Divergence: a fast moving average minus a slow one, with a signal line, to show momentum.

margin.def: The deposit needed to open and keep a leveraged position.

marginal rate.def: The rate charged on your next pound of income. Higher than your average rate, because lower slices of pay are taxed less.

market.def: Anywhere buyers and sellers meet to agree a price.

market cap.def: A company's total stock market value: share price × number of shares.

market order.def: An order to buy or sell now at the best available price.

minimum payment trap.def: Paying only a card's minimum, so most of each payment is interest and the debt lasts for years.

money.def: Anything people accept in exchange for goods and services. In the UK that's pounds, mostly held as numbers in bank accounts rather than notes and coins.

moving average.def: The average closing price over the last N periods, recalculated each period. Smooths noise but lags.

mpc.def: The Monetary Policy Committee: nine people at the Bank of England who vote on Bank Rate eight times a year.

national insurance.def: A deduction from pay over a threshold that builds your record for the State Pension and some benefits.

net interest margin.def: The gap between the interest a bank earns on loans and pays on deposits, as a share of its lending.

net pay.def: Take-home pay: what reaches your bank account after tax, National Insurance, pension and any student loan.

nominal return.def: The return shown on your statement, before taking inflation into account.

ocf.def: Ongoing charges figure: a fund's yearly running cost as a % of what you hold, taken automatically.

overconfidence.def: Believing you know more or can predict better than you can, leading to over-trading and concentrated bets.

overdraft.def: Borrowing by letting your current account go below £0. Arranged overdrafts often cost around 40% a year.

overfitting.def: Tuning a strategy so closely to past data that it looks perfect on history and fails on new data.

p/e ratio.def: Share price ÷ earnings per share: how many years of today's profit you pay for each share.

paper trading.def: Practising trades with pretend money at real prices, recorded as if they were real.

passive investing.def: Tracking an index cheaply instead of trying to beat it.

paye.def: Pay As You Earn: your employer works out your income tax and National Insurance and pays it to HMRC each time you're paid.

payslip.def: The statement you get each payday showing gross pay, every deduction and net pay.

personal allowance.def: The income you can have each tax year before paying income tax: £12,570 for most people in 2026/27.

pitch book.def: A slide deck bankers use to win work: market analysis, ideas, valuation ranges and track record.

platform fee.def: What an investment app or website charges to hold your investments: a % of your pot or a flat fee.

position sizing.def: Choosing how much to buy so that if your stop is hit, you lose exactly the amount you planned.

pound-cost averaging.def: Investing a fixed amount regularly, so you buy more units when prices are low and fewer when high.

present value.def: What future money is worth today: the future amount ÷ (1 + discount rate) for each year of waiting.

principal.def: The amount you start with, before any interest is added.

private equity.def: Firms that buy whole companies, often with borrowed money, run them for years and sell them.

profit.def: What's left from revenue after costs. Gross, operating and net profit take off more costs at each step.

qe.def: Quantitative easing: the central bank creating money to buy government bonds, pushing down long-term interest rates.

r-multiple.def: A trade's result divided by the amount risked: +2R made twice the risk; −1R hit the stop.

real return.def: What you gain in spending power after inflation. Roughly the nominal rate minus inflation; exactly (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.

rebalancing.def: Selling some of what has grown and buying what has lagged, to return a portfolio to its target mix.

recency bias.def: Giving too much weight to what just happened, as if recent returns predict the future.

regulator.def: A body that sets and enforces rules for firms, such as the FCA, the PRA and the Bank of England.

rent.def: What you pay a landlord to live in a home. In England, deposits are capped at five weeks' rent and must be protected.

resistance.def: A price level where rises have repeatedly stalled, because sellers stepped in.

retail bank.def: A bank serving the public: current accounts, savings, mortgages, loans and payments.

revenue.def: Money from sales before any costs are taken off. Also called turnover or the top line.

risk premium.def: The extra expected return investors demand for taking more risk, such as shares over cash.

risk/reward.def: The distance to your target divided by the distance to your stop, such as 2 : 1.

rsi.def: Relative Strength Index: recent gains versus losses on a 0–100 scale. Above 70 is called overbought, below 30 oversold.

rule of 72.def: A shortcut: 72 ÷ the yearly rate ≈ how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, about 12 years.

self-assessment.def: The yearly tax return for income HMRC doesn't already tax through PAYE, such as self-employed profit over £1,000.

sell side.def: Firms that sell financial services and products to investors, mainly investment banks and brokers.

share.def: A small piece of ownership in a company, also called a stock or equity.

simple interest.def: Interest worked out only on the original principal, so it's the same every year.

sipp.def: Self-Invested Personal Pension: a pension you open and manage yourself, with the same tax relief.

speculation.def: Buying or selling to profit from short-term price moves rather than to own a business for its long-term returns.

spread.def: The gap between the bid and ask prices: a cost on every round-trip trade.

spread bet.def: A leveraged bet of an amount per point of price movement. Usually free of UK Capital Gains Tax because it counts as gambling.

state pension.def: A regular payment from the government from State Pension age, based on your National Insurance record.

stock exchange.def: A regulated marketplace where shares are bought and sold, such as the London Stock Exchange.

stocks and shares isa.def: An ISA that holds investments such as funds and shares. Gains and dividends are tax-free; the value can fall.

stop order.def: An order that becomes a market order once the price reaches your level. Used for stop-losses.

stop-loss.def: A pre-set exit that closes a trade if the price moves against you to a chosen level.

strategy rules.def: Exact rules for market, entry, stop, exit, size and filters, clear enough that anyone would take the same trades.

student loan plans.def: The repayment rules for your loan. Plan 5 (England, courses from 2023): 9% of income above £25,000, written off after 40 years.

sunk cost.def: Money or time already spent that can't be recovered. It shouldn't drive future decisions.

support.def: A price level where falls have repeatedly stopped, because buyers stepped in.

synergies.def: Cost savings or extra sales a buyer expects from combining two companies.

tax code.def: Tells your employer how much tax-free pay you get. 1257L means £12,570 a year, the standard Personal Allowance.

tax relief.def: Income tax given back on pension contributions, so each £1 in your pot costs a basic-rate taxpayer about 80p.

tilt.def: Frustration after losses that makes a trader abandon their rules: bigger, faster, revenge trades.

time horizon.def: How long you plan to hold an investment or trade, from minutes to decades.

timeframe.def: How much time each candle or bar covers on a chart, from a minute to a week or more.

total return.def: An investment's price change plus dividends or interest, as if reinvested. The fair way to compare investments.

trading allowance.def: Up to £1,000 a year of income from self-employment or side hustles that you don't need to declare or pay tax on.

trading hours.def: When a market is open. The London Stock Exchange is 8am–4.30pm; US markets about 2.30pm–9pm UK time.

trading journal.def: A record of every trade: the plan, entry, stop, target, size, result in R and whether you followed your rules.

transmission mechanism.def: The chain from a Bank Rate change to bank rates, spending, demand and finally inflation.

trend.def: The general direction of prices: up (higher highs and lows), down, or sideways.

variable rate.def: An interest rate the bank can change at any time. Most easy-access savings accounts have one.

volatility.def: How much an investment's price swings up and down. A common way to measure risk.

volume.def: How many shares or contracts traded in a period. High volume suggests more conviction behind a move.

win rate.def: The share of trades that make money. Meaningless without the size of wins and losses.

workplace pension.def: A pension your employer sets up, which you and your employer pay into while you work.

yield.def: The yearly return from a bond bought at today's price and held to maturity, counting coupons and the gain or loss to face value.

yield curve.def: A chart of yields on one issuer's bonds against how long they have to run. Usually slopes upwards.
